lines: Second Vinnie Vincent Invasion album, pairing Vinnie Vincent's flashy guitar work with a slicker late-1980s hard-rock production and stronger hooks than the debut. It pushes the band toward melodic metal while still leaving room for long solos and fretboard excess.

Ace Frehley's first all-new solo studio album in many years, returning him to a straightforward hard-rock setting built on riffs, leads, and dry humor. It balances classic Space Ace attitude with a more modern, compact production.

Gene Simmons's second solo album. One of its best-known moments is "Firestarter," a cover of The Prodigy's song that was also promoted with a music video and features Dave Navarro on guitar. The album overall plays like a personality-driven showcase centered on Simmons's voice, image, and taste for stylistic variety.

Bruce Kulick solo release built around guitar-centered instrumentals and melodic hard-rock workouts. It highlights his clean phrasing, layered leads, and studio-minded approach outside the Kiss framework.
Badlands debut album, fusing bluesy hard rock with a heavier late-1980s edge. Features Ray Gillen and Eric Singer, who previously played together in Black Sabbath.

Bruce Kulick's third solo album combines melodic hard rock with a broad guest list and a more song-focused approach than his earlier instrumental work. It keeps his guitar at the center while giving the material a collaborative feel.

Blackjack's debut album featuring Bruce Kulick is rooted in late-1970s hard rock with touches of AOR and soul. The record is driven by sharp guitar work, strong hooks, and an early Michael Bolton vocal performance.

Black 'n Blue's debut album featuring Tommy Thayer is built on catchy Sunset Strip hard rock with a lean power-pop streak. It is polished and hooky, but still guitar-forward enough to show why the band stood out.

A six-track 2025 reunion release from Tommy Thayer and Jaime St. James, written together in the same melodic hard rock lane that shaped their late-1980s work. Produced by Rob Daiker and cut in Portland.

Alice Cooper album featuring Eric Singer on drums, built around a darker industrial-metal palette and a more confrontational lyrical tone. It trades classic shock-rock fun for a heavier, more modern attack.
Peter Criss comeback album that recasts him in a tougher early-1990s hard-rock setting. It keeps his raspy voice up front while giving the songs a heavier punch than much of his earlier solo work.
With the self-titled Chelsea release in 1970, Peter Criss is the only Kiss member to have played on a full album pre Kiss.

Vinnie Vincent release built around high-drama vocals, dense guitars, and the over-the-top melodic metal style closely associated with his post-Kiss work. It feels like a maximalist guitar record first and a band record second.

Ace Frehley's first post-Kiss offering reintroduces him with brighter production, radio-minded hooks, and plenty of lead guitar. It updates his sound for the late 1980s without losing the swagger that defined his Kiss-era writing.
Recorded by Kulick/Katz/Bois in 1974. This 2015 release adds the new title track "Got To Get Back" and includes remixed and remastered songs from their 1974 sessions.
Good Rats album featuring Bruce Kulick on lead guitar.

Black 'n Blue album featuring Tommy Thayer, pushing the band toward a glossier mid-1980s metal sound without losing its knack for hooks. The record sits comfortably between radio-friendly polish and riff-driven hard rock.

Peter Criss solo album that moves between melodic rock, radio-friendly polish, and his grittier vocal instincts. It is more controlled and streamlined than his earlier work, but still unmistakably built around his voice.

Disco project featuring Eric Carr on drums and backing vocals, before his Kiss years. Credited under his birth name Paul Caravello. Released 14-08-1979 on Casablanca, it was produced by Lewis Merenstein and Ralph Moss and recorded/mixed at The Sound Place, New York. The album pairs long-form dance grooves with melodic vocal hooks and polished late-1970s arrangements.

Paul Stanley's second solo album that plays like a modern melodic-rock record rather than a Kiss side project. It emphasizes polished songwriting, strong choruses, and a cleaner, more contemporary production style.

ESP release featuring Eric Singer and Bruce Kulick, capturing a tough late-1990s hard-rock sound with a direct, no-frills band feel. It works as a side-project snapshot of two seasoned Kiss players cutting loose together.

Mark St. John collection that serves as both a showcase and a memorial, emphasizing his flashy technique and melodic hard-rock instincts. The material underlines how distinctive his playing remained outside his brief Kiss chapter.

Mark St. John Project EP featuring Mark St. John on guitars, with Phil Naro on lead vocals, Roger Banks on drums, Stan Miczek on bass, and Chris Sevdalis on grand piano and keyboards on "No, I'm Not Afraid".

Black 'n Blue album featuring Tommy Thayer, sharpening the band's glam-metal side with bigger choruses and a heavier studio sheen. It aims squarely at mid-1980s commercial hard rock while keeping the guitars prominent.
Soul Station album led by Paul Stanley, stepping away from hard rock in favor of classic soul, R&B, and horn-driven arrangements. Features both covers and originals.

Released in 2007 on Megaforce Records, Peter Criss's fifth solo studio album. It leans into blues, soul, and singer-songwriter influences more than straight hard rock. Personal and unforced, with the songs built around voice, groove, and atmosphere.

Ace Frehley covers album that doubles as a tribute to his musical roots and a reminder of how naturally his guitar personality fits classic rock material. The performances are loose, affectionate, and built around feel over polish.

Second volume of Ace Frehley's covers project, again pairing his signature guitar tone with songs that shaped him before and alongside Kiss. Musicians on the record include Jeremy Ashbrock, Ryan Spencer Cook, Bruce Kulick, Rob Sabino, Alex Salzman, Philip Shouse, Paul Simmons and Matt Starr.
Peter's first post-Kiss album, released on Casablanca Records. Recording began while Criss was still officially a member of Kiss. Musicians include Stan Penridge, Tony Mercandante and Benny Harrison.
Peter Criss released his well-received sixth solo album in 2025. 11 rock songs written by Peter himself, composed with Mike McLaughlin.

A posthumous collection of Eric Carr demos from 1986-1989, centered on songs developed with Bruce Kulick and Adam Mitchell. It blends polished demo production with raw work-tape energy, and highlights Carr as more than a drummer through his lead vocals, guitars, bass, and keyboards across the sessions.

Second Frehley's Comet album, keeping Ace in a more polished late-1980s melodic metal lane while retaining his identifiable guitar phrasing. It is slicker and more streamlined than some fans prefer, but still carries his stamp.

Black Sabbath release featuring Eric Singer on drums. Originally intended as a solo album, but Warner Bros. Records insisting on a Black Sabbath album, it was billed as Black Sabbath featuring Tony Iommi.

Ace Frehley solo album that reconnects with the direct riffing, vocal swagger, and lead-guitar personality fans expect from him. It keeps the production modern enough to sound current without sanding off his rough edges.

Ace Frehley album built on concise riffs, strong choruses, and a confident late-career guitar performance. It feels like a focused solo statement from an artist comfortable leaning into the parts of his identity fans want most.

Union album featuring Bruce Kulick, built around muscular hard rock, big hooks, and a band-first chemistry. It lets Kulick stretch as both guitarist and writer outside the stylistic boundaries of Kiss.

Black Sabbath album featuring Eric Singer on drums, balancing doomier atmosphere with a cleaner late-1980s metal production. It marks a reset period for the band, with disciplined drumming and a more dramatic vocal style.

Five archival songs by Tommy Thayer and Jamie St. James, recorded in late 1988/early 1989 and finally issued in 2022 as a self-released CD. The core lineup is Thayer (guitars) and St. James (vocals, drums), with guest parts by Jeff Labansky, Mitch Perry, and Patrick Young. The material was restored from surviving DAT and cassette sources after the original analog tapes had deteriorated beyond use.

Bruce Kulick solo release that continues his melodic hard-rock and guitar-instrumental path with a polished studio sound. The focus stays on tone, phrasing, and layered arrangements rather than flash for its own sake.
Treasure album featuring Vinnie Vincent, aka Vinnie Cusano, on vocals, lead guitar, and 12-string guitar. Produced by Felix Cavaliere.

Ace Frehley solo album that pushes harder and meaner than some of his earlier post-Kiss work, with thick riffs and a tougher street-level hard-rock tone. It is one of his stronger records for balancing attitude, humor, and lead guitar.

Union debut featuring Bruce Kulick, combining late-1990s hard-rock muscle with strong vocal melodies and a purposeful band identity. It gives Kulick room to riff, solo, and co-drive the material rather than simply decorate it.

Vinnie Vincent Invasion debut album is overflowing with fretboard heroics, theatrical vocals, and the excesses of mid-1980s metal. The songwriting often exists to frame Vinnie Vincent's guitar personality, which is exactly the point.

White Tiger's self-titled debut from former Kiss guitarist Mark St. John, featuring David Donato on vocals, Michael Norton on bass, and Brian James Fox on drums. Produced by Mark St. John, recorded at Front Page Studios, and mixed at the new Record Plant.

Black 'n Blue album featuring Tommy Thayer, leaning into glossy hooks and radio-minded choruses without abandoning the guitars. It is one of the band's clearest examples of accessible hard rock done with style.

Second Blackjack album featuring Bruce Kulick, moving the band further toward slick AOR and polished songcraft. It keeps the guitar work sharp while giving equal weight to melody and vocal presentation.
